topic: Research why films dont look like films anymore and use jurassic park as an example

thesis.text: Audiences are openly complaining that modern movies look flat, dull, and sludgy despite having the biggest budgets ever, and the sources agree it's not really the CGI or the digital cameras themselves, it's how filmmakers are choosing to use them. Jurassic Park still gets held up as the gold standard because Spielberg used the new technology as little as possible, about 50 fully digital shots total, and hid the rest behind animatronics, rain, and motion blur.

claims.title: Everybody's noticing the same thing: movies with the biggest budgets ever look flat, plastic, and cheap.
claims.what_sources_say: Both YouTube essays open with basically the same complaint: movies with bigger budgets than film has ever seen still look flat, plastic, and cheap, and some TV shows look more cinematic than what's playing in theaters. The Stage 32 comment thread backs this up too, with a working cinematographer wondering out loud why movies from the 80s, 90s, and early 2000s look better than what's coming out now. It's not a fringe gripe, it's the starting point for three separate pieces of content.
claims.my_read: This is the hook that gets people watching, and it's genuinely three separate groups landing on the same complaint, which is worth more than one person's pet peeve.
claims.say_it_like: Movies have never had bigger budgets, and somehow they've never looked cheaper.

confidence.reason: Two independent video essays and a working cinematographers' comment thread all open with the same complaint, without citing each other.

claims.title: The two main video essays agree: CGI, digital cameras, and AI are not actually why movies look different now.
claims.what_sources_say: Both essayists go out of their way to knock down the easy answer. One says straight up that digital cameras themselves are not the reason movies look boring, and the other calls CGI, visual effects, AI, and filters scapegoats rather than the real cause. One of them even backs it up with a specific example: Superbad was shot on a digital camera with less dynamic range than an iPhone, but it still looks great because of a red car and deliberate 1970s-style brown, wood-paneled interiors.
claims.my_read: This is the pivot the whole story needs. If you let the audience blame 'CGI' and stop there, you don't have a video, you have a rant. This claim is what earns everything that follows.
claims.say_it_like: It's not the CGI's fault, it's what people are choosing to do with it.

confidence.reason: Two separate creators make the identical argument without referencing each other, and one backs it with a concrete, checkable example.

claims.title: Plenty of movies still look great right now, which proves the tools aren't the problem.
claims.what_sources_say: One essayist lists Dune, The Substance, Smile, Nosferatu, and The Brutalist as proof modern cinematography can absolutely look good, calling The Brutalist one of the best-looking films of the decade. Over on the Stage 32 comment thread, a working filmmaker separately singles out Nosferatu for the same reason, praising Robert Eggers and cinematographer Blaschke for giving audiences still frames worth sitting with. Two different sources land on the same film as the counterexample.
claims.pushback: This cuts against any argument that says the whole industry has lost the ability to shoot well. If Nosferatu can look like that, the skill hasn't disappeared, it's just not being used everywhere.
claims.my_read: This is the detail that keeps the whole video honest. It's not 'movies are dead,' it's 'most movies aren't trying,' and that's a much more useful claim to build a video around.
claims.say_it_like: Nosferatu looks incredible, so don't tell me the tools can't do it anymore.

confidence.reason: Two sources independently praise Nosferatu specifically, though the wider list of 'good-looking' films only comes from one of them.

claims.title: Modern cameras can capture so much light and shadow now that filmmakers show everything, and that's what makes the image look flat and gray.
claims.what_sources_say: Both essays land here independently. One calls it a 'gray sludgy aesthetic' created by high dynamic range cameras, while the other describes filmmakers obsessing over maximizing dynamic range so nothing clips, keeping the whole image inside a narrow 10 to 90 percent exposure range. The argument in both cases is the same: just because a camera can capture everything doesn't mean a film should show everything, because real contrast, like stepping outside and being blinded, is what the human eye actually experiences.
claims.my_read: This is the single clearest, most testable idea in the whole pile of research, and it's the one I'd build the video's visual demonstration around.
claims.say_it_like: Cameras got so good at seeing in the dark and the light that filmmakers forgot contrast was ever the point.

confidence.reason: Two separate essayists give the same technical explanation using different camera specs and different films as examples, and neither seems to be quoting the other.

claims.title: Lighting itself got softer and lazier, with filmmakers leaning on high ISO instead of actually lighting the scene.
claims.what_sources_say: One essay walks through this in detail: softboxes, domes, china balls, and book lights replaced the harsh, hard lighting that used to carve out shape and texture, and cleaner high-ISO sensors let filmmakers skip lighting dim scenes altogether, which is why some modern night scenes look like night-vision footage instead of the deliberately lit blue night scenes in something like Lord of the Rings. The other essay backs this up from a different angle, saying the industry is losing the taste to light a scene like David Fincher's Se7en, and that teaching someone to light a green screen takes about 20 minutes.
claims.my_read: The green screen line is the detail that will actually land with people. Twenty minutes to light something versus the days it takes to properly light a real set says everything about where the effort is going.
claims.say_it_like: Why light a room properly when you can just crank the ISO and fix it later?

confidence.reason: Both essays describe the same shift away from deliberate lighting, but with different specifics, so it's more a shared conclusion than a shared data point.

claims.title: Wide lenses and constantly moving cameras make modern shots feel like a vlog or a video game instead of a composed film.
claims.what_sources_say: One essay lays out the mechanics: bigger sensors and wider lenses pull the camera physically closer to actors, breaking the distant, eye-level framing traditional cinema used, and cheap digital recording plus lightweight gimbals and drones mean cameras never stop moving, which can make a shot feel like a video game rather than cinema. It's mostly a one-source technical argument, but it lines up with a much more casual complaint from a Stage 32 commenter, who separately calls out shaky cam as nauseating when it's overused.
claims.my_read: This is a case where the polished technical explanation and the blunt gut reaction from a working filmmaker are describing the same thing from two different altitudes, which makes me trust it more than either alone.
claims.say_it_like: When the camera never stops moving and never steps back, it stops feeling like a movie and starts feeling like someone's vlog.

confidence.reason: The detailed technical breakdown comes from one source, but a separate comment thread flags the same symptom, constant camera movement, independently.

claims.title: Once a movie is built around thousands of VFX shots and green screens, nobody on set commits to a final look anymore, because it might all get changed later.
claims.what_sources_say: This one shows up from several directions. One essayist points out that TV shows with 2,000 to 3,000 VFX shots make it hard to commit to lighting because rooms and windows might get altered or removed in post, leading to bland, uncommitted images. A VFX artist writing about The Lost World makes almost the same point about modern movies leaning on green screens and virtual production volumes, saying it can make actors feel like they're not actually in an environment. The Stage 32 comment thread adds that colorists and post houses can sometimes wreck a good image after the fact, which is why some cinematographers now fight to sit in on their own color sessions. And the philosophy-flavored take on Jurassic World Rebirth argues that the shift from committing to an image on set to fixing it in post is a big part of why modern films feel fake, even when they use real locations.
claims.my_read: This is the connective tissue of the whole video. It's the actual mechanism behind the flat, sludgy look everyone's complaining about: not the tools, but the fact that nobody has to make a final decision on set anymore.
claims.say_it_like: When you can fix it in post, you stop deciding what the shot actually looks like on the day, and it shows.

confidence.reason: Four different sources, a video essayist, a VFX writer, a comment thread of working DPs, and a philosophy-focused essay, all describe the same fix-it-later problem from their own angle.

claims.title: Some cinematographers think this whole thing is really about money and algorithms, not artistic choices at all.
claims.what_sources_say: This one only comes from the Stage 32 comment thread, but it's a real pushback worth including: one commenter argues the video everyone's discussing doesn't consider the business side enough, and that today's visual style is driven more by financiers, the people holding the purse strings, and algorithms than by creative people making choices. Another commenter, Maurice Vaughan, agrees, and adds that indie films often look as good as older movies specifically because indie cinematographers have more creative freedom than people working inside the studio system.
claims.pushback: This is a direct counter to every 'filmmakers got lazy' argument above. If indie films with the same tools still look great, the problem might not be craft at all, it might be who's allowed to make the decisions.
claims.my_read: I'd treat this as the honest complication of the whole video, not a footnote. It's the difference between blaming artists and blaming the system they work inside.
claims.say_it_like: Maybe it's not that filmmakers forgot how to light a scene, maybe it's that nobody's letting them.

confidence.reason: This only comes from one comment thread on one article, and it's opinion from commenters, not something checked against actual production data.

claims.title: Jurassic Park is the film everyone points to as the gold standard, and the reason given again and again is that Spielberg barely used CGI at all.
claims.what_sources_say: This is the most repeated point across the whole pile of research. A VFX artist breaking down The Lost World says late-90s CGI wasn't advanced enough to use heavily, so Spielberg balanced practical effects with sparing digital work. Two separate history-style articles say the same thing: Spielberg originally planned to use only practical effects, stop-motion raptors and an animatronic T-Rex, and only added digital dinosaurs after ILM showed him test footage, with the finished film landing at about 50 shots of fully digital creatures. A film blog looking back twenty years later agrees, saying the filmmakers relied primarily on animatronics and used CGI only for creatures that couldn't be built practically.
claims.my_read: This is the one fact in this whole pile of research I'd bet money on. Four sources, made for completely different audiences, all land on the same number and the same story.
claims.say_it_like: The reason Jurassic Park still looks real is that it barely used the fake stuff.

confidence.reason: Four separate sources, a VFX-focused article, two history overviews, and a film blog, all independently describe the same practical-first, sparing-CGI approach and the roughly 50-shot figure.

claims.title: Because there were so few CGI shots, the crew could obsess over each one, and they hid the weak ones in rain, dusk, and motion blur.
claims.what_sources_say: One film blog lays this out in detail: using less CGI overall meant more attention could be lavished on every individual digital frame, and the effects team hid key CGI sequences in low light, the T-Rex chasing the jeep in the rain, the T-Rex and raptor fight in a dim park building, the brachiosaurs at sunset. The one big effects sequence shot in full daylight, the gallimimus stampede, hides its seams with speed and motion blur instead of darkness. This only comes from one source, but a reader comment on the same piece backs it up with a comparison to how Disney's Dinosaur ride hides its animatronics in the dark for the same reason.
claims.my_read: This is the detail I'd want on screen side by side, the rainy T-Rex chase against a modern CGI creature standing in broad daylight. It's the clearest visual proof of the whole argument.
claims.say_it_like: Spielberg didn't fix his CGI's weak spots, he just never let you see them in the light.

confidence.reason: This comes from a single film blog, and though a reader comment on that same post offers a supporting comparison, it's really one source telling a consistent story rather than independent corroboration.

claims.title: Modern movies flip that ratio: CGI is everywhere in full daylight, and the artists making it are spread way too thin.
claims.what_sources_say: The VFX artist writing about The Lost World says movies that use CGI for everything place a huge burden on artists working under tight deadlines, and that spreading artists thin across thousands of shots leads to an overall drop in quality, because the meticulous shot-by-shot planning the original Jurassic Park team did tends to get abandoned. The film blog adds that modern blockbusters with CGI in every frame don't get the low-light or motion-blur cover Jurassic Park used, so their effects have to hold up in plain view, with nowhere to hide.
claims.my_read: This is basically the production-side mirror of the audience complaint that opened the whole video. More shots, less time each, no hiding spot, worse result. It's not mysterious.
claims.say_it_like: You can't give a thousand shots the same love Spielberg gave fifty.

confidence.reason: Two sources make the same point about scale and workload, though neither cites actual numbers for a modern film's shot count or schedule.

claims.title: In 1993 audiences would not have forgiven bad dinosaurs, but today's audiences are so used to CGI that mediocre effects barely hurt a movie.
claims.what_sources_say: This is a single film blog's argument, but it's a sharp one: by 2013 audiences were so used to CGI that even bad effects just fade into the background, so weak effects work in something like The Avengers or The Hobbit doesn't cost those films a penny at the box office. Back in 1993 there was no such acceptance, so the Jurassic Park team had to spend maximum time, energy, and money getting the dinosaurs exactly right, because a bad effect back then would have been a real problem.
claims.pushback: This is a big claim to hang on one blog post from 2013, and it doesn't have any box office or audience survey data behind it, it's an assertion, not a measurement.
claims.my_read: I actually buy the logic even without the receipts, because it explains something the other claims don't, why there's less external pressure on studios to fix the workload and scale problems above. But say it as a theory, not a fact.
claims.say_it_like: Nobody in 1993 was going to shrug off a fake-looking dinosaur, but we shrug off fake CGI every week now.

confidence.reason: This whole argument rests on one blog post's claim about audience tolerance, with no box office data or survey cited to back it up.

claims.title: The 'realness' gap has less to do with how much CGI a film uses and more to do with deep focus, film grain, and literal light hitting film versus a sensor converting it, one video essay argues.
claims.what_sources_say: This is a single article covering one video essayist's argument, but it's a genuinely different angle from everything else here. It claims older films used more deep focus, keeping backgrounds sharp so your eyes could scan the frame the way you scan a real room, while modern shallow-focus shots don't work that way. It also leans on the idea that celluloid is authentic because light physically struck the film, while a digital sensor just converts light into data. To make the point concrete, it compares the sweaty, struggling actors in Sorcerer from 1977 to a similar humid scene in Jurassic World Rebirth, where flat lighting and clean makeup make the actors look comfortable instead of authentic.
claims.pushback: This is a much more academic, philosophy-driven argument than the camera and lighting explanations from the other essays, and it never really reconciles with them. It's possible both are true at once, but nobody in the sources tries to connect the two.
claims.my_read: I'd use this as the emotional close of the video rather than a technical point, because it's not really arguing about specs, it's arguing that a movie has to feel like something happened to real people in a real place, and Jurassic Park managed that in a way the newer film in the same franchise apparently doesn't.
claims.say_it_like: It's not just how much CGI a film uses, it's whether it still feels like light actually touched something real.

confidence.reason: This entire argument comes from a single article summarizing one YouTube essayist's video, with no other source engaging with these specific ideas.

story_goods.text: Superbad was shot on the Panavision Genesis HD camera, which had less dynamic range than an iPhone, but its strong look came from a red car and 1970s-style mahogany-wood, brown-carpet interiors.
Eggers' Nosferatu was terrific to me because of all the gorgeous still frames he and Blaschke created where the audience could sit with them and let the images resonate.
In The Lost World, visceral moments like the T-Rex's tongue were achieved with practical effects rather than CGI.
Jurassic Park features about 50 shots of digital-only prehistoric creatures, including the first full-body dinosaur shot ever, the Brachiosaurus.
a perfect collision of coming-of-age computer generated imagery... with state of the art puppetry
The VFX team hid key CGI sequences in low light: the T-Rex chasing the jeep in the rain, and the T-Rex fighting raptors in the dusky park headquarters.
The gallimimus stampede, the one major effects sequence shot in full daylight, hides its flaws with high speed and motion blur instead of darkness.

Van der Linden compares the gritty, sweaty shots of Sorcerer (1977), starring Roy Scheider, to a similar humid, tropical scene in Jurassic World Rebirth, where flat lighting and vanity makeup make the actors look comfortable rather than authentic.
The speaker says teaching someone to light a green screen takes only about 20 minutes.
TV shows with 2,000 to 3,000 VFX shots make it hard to commit to lighting choices, because rooms and windows may be altered or removed later.

holes.missing: nobody actually asked a VFX artist working on a current blockbuster why crews are stretched thin or why studios greenlight thousand-shot movies
holes.hurts_because: the whole 'artists are spread too thin' claim is asserted by outside writers, not by anyone who's actually sat in that chair, so a sharp viewer will ask how anyone would know
holes.how_to_fill: Find a VFX artist or supervisor, maybe through r/vfx or a trade outlet like Cartoon Brew, and just ask them what a typical shot count and deadline looks like on a modern tentpole.

holes.missing: no cinematographer or director working today defending the soft, flat modern look with their own reasoning
holes.hurts_because: right now every voice in this video is a critic, so it plays as one-sided even if the criticism is fair, and a real pushback would actually make the argument stronger
holes.how_to_fill: Look for interviews with a current blockbuster's DP about their color grading choices or camera pick, ideally someone explaining an HDR-first workflow.

holes.missing: nobody from the studio or financing side is in here explaining the business logic behind these choices
holes.hurts_because: claim 8 blames financiers and algorithms but only ever hears from cinematographers complaining about them, so it's a one-sided account of a fight we only see one side of
holes.how_to_fill: Chase a producer or studio executive interview, or a trade piece in Variety or The Hollywood Reporter about how a modern tentpole's visual style gets approved.

holes.missing: no actual shot-count or budget comparison between Jurassic Park and a modern blockbuster of similar scale
holes.hurts_because: the whole 'they used fewer shots and had more time' argument would hit so much harder with real numbers side by side instead of 'about 50 shots' from one movie and vague 'thousands' from another
holes.how_to_fill: Look for a making-of book or VFX trade retrospective, like Cinefex archives, that lists actual shot counts and schedules for Jurassic Park and a comparable modern film.

holes.missing: nothing here about how people actually watch movies now, on a phone, a laptop, or an HDR TV, and whether that's shaping how films get graded
holes.hurts_because: if colorists are grading for ten different screen types instead of one dark cinema, that could explain a lot of the flat, safe look, and none of these sources even raise it
holes.how_to_fill: Find an interview with a working colorist about grading for Dolby Vision, HDR10, and standard screens at the same time.

sections.title: Movies with the biggest budgets ever are being called flat, plastic, and cheap-looking
sections.body: The complaint that starts most of this material is the same one: films now have more money behind them than film has ever had, and yet a lot of them look flat, plastic, and cheap on screen. Some television shows now look more cinematic than what's playing in theaters, a complaint that opens two separate YouTube video essays on the subject, one titled "Why don't movies look like *movies* anymore?" and another titled "Why Movies Don't Look Like Movies Anymore." Why films from the 1980s, 1990s, and early 2000s still look better than what's coming out now is a question one working director of photography wonders aloud in a comment thread of working cinematographers in the Stage 32 Cinematography Lounge. Nobody in this material treats it as a fringe opinion; it is the question each piece sets out to answer.

sections.title: CGI and digital cameras are not actually why modern movies look different, according to both major video essays on the topic
sections.body:
The easy answer gets rejected outright by both video essays. One states plainly that digital cameras themselves are not the reason movies look boring. The other calls CGI, visual effects, AI, and filters scapegoats rather than the real cause. Superbad was shot on a Panavision Genesis HD camera with less dynamic range than an iPhone and it still looks good, thanks to choices like a red car in frame and deliberately 1970s-style mahogany-wood, brown-carpeted interiors, an example one essay uses to back this up.

The same argument shows up as a list of counterexamples. Dune, The Substance, Smile, Nosferatu, and The Brutalist are cited by one essayist as films shot in the last few years that look good, with The Brutalist singled out as one of the best-looking films of the decade. On the Stage 32 comment thread, a working filmmaker separately singles out Nosferatu for the same reason, praising director Robert Eggers and cinematographer Jarin Blaschke for creating still frames the audience can sit with and let resonate. The same film comes up independently in two different sources, without either referencing the other. The point both are making is that the tools have not lost the ability to produce a good image; something else is missing.

sections.title: Cameras can now capture so much light and shadow that filmmakers show everything, and that is what produces the gray, flat look people are complaining about
sections.body:
The same technical explanation is reached independently by both video essays. One describes it as a "gray sludgy aesthetic" produced by high dynamic range cameras. The other describes filmmakers obsessing over maximizing dynamic range so nothing in the image clips into pure black or pure white, keeping the whole picture inside a narrow exposure band, roughly 10 to 90 percent of the range available.

The argument in both cases is the same: a camera being able to capture everything is not a reason to show everything. Real contrast, like the moment of stepping outside on a bright day and being briefly blinded, is what the human eye actually experiences, and modern digital workflows tend to flatten that experience out rather than preserve it. The same technical description gets reached using different camera specifications and different films as examples, with neither essay appearing to draw on the other.

sections.title: Lighting got softer and cameras got closer and shakier, and both changes are described as choices rather than limitations
sections.body:
Softboxes, light domes, china balls, and book lights have replaced the harder, more directional lighting that used to carve shape and texture into a face or a room, a shift one video essay traces in how scenes get lit. Cleaner high-ISO camera sensors let filmmakers skip lighting dim scenes at all, which is why some modern night scenes end up looking closer to night-vision footage than to the deliberately lit blue-tinted night scenes in something like The Lord of the Rings. The same essay makes the point with a blunt comparison: teaching someone to light a green screen takes about 20 minutes, while the industry is said to be losing the patience, or the taste, to light a scene the way David Fincher lit Se7en.

A separate technical argument covers the camera itself. Bigger sensors and wider lenses pull the camera physically closer to actors, breaking the more distant, eye-level framing traditional cinema relied on. Cheap digital recording combined with lightweight gimbals and drones means the camera rarely stops moving, which can make a shot feel closer to a video game than to a composed film frame. A Stage 32 commenter, working independently of that essay, raises the same symptom from a viewer's seat, calling overused shaky cam nauseating.

sections.title: When a film is built around thousands of visual effects shots, nobody on set has to commit to a final look, because it might all change later
sections.body:
This idea comes at from several directions. Television shows carrying 2,000 to 3,000 VFX shots make it hard for anyone to commit to a lighting setup, since a room or a window might be altered or removed entirely once the effects team gets to it, producing bland, uncommitted-looking images, as one video essayist points out. A VFX artist writing about The Lost World: Jurassic Park makes a related point about current productions leaning on green screens and virtual production volumes, arguing it can leave actors feeling like they are not actually standing in an environment.

The Stage 32 comment thread adds a production detail: colorists and post-production houses can sometimes undo a carefully shot image after the fact, which is why some cinematographers now insist on sitting in on their own color-grading sessions. This shift, from committing to an image on set to fixing it later in post-production, is a major reason modern films feel fake even when they're shot on real locations, according to a separate article on the philosophy of Jurassic World Rebirth.

sections.title: Some working cinematographers argue this is really about financiers and algorithms, not artistic laziness
sections.body:
This argument appears in one place, the Stage 32 comment thread, but it directly challenges every craft-based explanation offered elsewhere. One commenter argues that the discussion of the video everyone is reacting to leaves out the business side entirely, and that today's visual style is shaped more by financiers, the people controlling the budget, and by algorithms than by the creative decisions of directors and cinematographers. Another commenter, Maurice Vaughan, agrees and adds a specific comparison: indie films often look as good as older studio films precisely because indie cinematographers have more creative freedom than people working inside the studio system.

The implication is a direct counter to the idea that filmmakers simply stopped trying. If a cinematographer working outside the studio system, with the same lenses and the same cameras, can still produce a strong image, the missing ingredient may not be skill or effort at all. It may be who is allowed to make the decision.

sections.title: Jurassic Park kept its digital dinosaurs to about 50 shots and hid nearly all of them in rain, dusk, or motion blur, and the material argues modern films do the opposite
sections.body:
The most repeated fact across this material is that Steven Spielberg originally planned to shoot Jurassic Park using only practical effects, stop-motion raptors and a full-size animatronic Tyrannosaurus rex, and only added computer-generated dinosaurs after Industrial Light & Magic showed him test footage. The finished film landed at roughly 50 shots of fully digital creatures, including what is described as the first full-body digital dinosaur shot ever committed to film, the Brachiosaurus. A VFX artist writing separately about the sequel, The Lost World, notes that late-1990s CGI simply was not advanced enough to lean on heavily, which is why even a visceral moment like the T-Rex's tongue was done practically rather than digitally, and why the team balanced practical work with sparing digital shots.

A film blog looking back at the original film explains what that scarcity bought the production: because there were so few fully digital shots, the effects team could lavish attention on each individual frame, and they hid the weaker ones in low light. The Tyrannosaurus chasing the jeep happens in rain. The Tyrannosaurus fighting the raptors happens inside a dim park building. The brachiosaurs are shown at sunset. The one major effects sequence shot in full daylight, the gallimimus stampede, hides its seams with speed and motion blur instead of darkness.

The same VFX artist argues that modern productions do close to the opposite. Movies that lean on CGI for every shot place a heavy burden on artists working under tight deadlines, and spreading artists across thousands of shots tends to lower overall quality, because the kind of meticulous, shot-by-shot planning the original Jurassic Park crew did gets abandoned. The film blog adds that modern blockbusters using CGI in nearly every frame do not get the low-light or motion-blur cover Jurassic Park used, so their effects have to hold up in plain view, with nowhere left to hide.

sections.title: If audiences no longer punish bad effects, that removes one of the pressures that used to force careful work, which lines up with the claim that financiers now drive the visual style
sections.body:
One film blog argues that audience tolerance for CGI has changed the incentives. By the time of writing, audiences had grown so used to computer-generated imagery that even weak effects work, in something like The Avengers or The Hobbit, does not cost those films at the box office; the flaws just fade into the background. Back in 1993 there was no such acceptance, so the Jurassic Park team had to spend maximum time, money, and attention getting the dinosaurs right, because a bad effect then would have been a real problem. This claim comes from a single blog post with no box office data or audience survey behind it; it is an assertion about audience behavior, not a measurement of it.

Separately, a Stage 32 comment thread argues that today's visual style is driven more by financiers and algorithms than by the creative choices of directors and cinematographers, and that indie films often look better than studio films specifically because indie cinematographers have more freedom from that system. No source puts these two claims side by side, but they fit together in an obvious way: if audiences no longer punish a flat or sloppy image, the people controlling a film's budget have less market pressure to insist on the kind of obsessive, shot-by-shot craft the Jurassic Park team applied. That connection isn't made explicitly by either source; it remains an inference rather than something either piece argues directly.

sections.title: Two different explanations for why modern footage feels less real are never weighed against each other in this material
sections.body:
One explanation is technical and about exposure: modern cameras can capture such a wide range of light and shadow that filmmakers choose to show all of it, keeping the image inside a narrow, evenly-lit exposure band instead of letting parts of the frame go properly dark or properly bright, which produces the flat, gray look several sources describe. The argument is that a camera being capable of capturing everything is not a reason to display everything, since real human vision includes genuine contrast, like being briefly blinded on stepping outside into sunlight.

A separate, more philosophical explanation, covered in an article about one video essayist's argument, says the realness gap has less to do with exposure and more to do with deep focus and the physical difference between film and a digital sensor: older films kept backgrounds sharp so the eye could scan a frame the way it scans a real room, and celluloid is treated as more authentic because light physically struck the film stock, while a digital sensor only converts light into data. That argument is made concrete by comparing the sweaty, straining actors of Sorcerer, a 1977 film starring Roy Scheider, to a similarly humid scene in Jurassic World Rebirth, where flat lighting and clean makeup leave the actors looking comfortable rather than authentic.

Modern footage feeling less real is the complaint both explanations are trying to account for, though neither source engages with the other's argument. It is possible both mechanisms are operating on the same footage at once, one about exposure and one about focus and material, but nothing in this material tries to reconcile them or say which one is doing more of the work.

noticings.text: A single film blog, "Four Reasons Why Jurassic Park's Visuals Still Amaze," supplies some of the sharpest details in the whole set, the rain-and-dusk hiding technique, the gallimimus motion-blur trick, and the theory about audience tolerance for bad CGI, and none of these appear in any other source, though the underlying events are independently checkable.

The claim that modern cinematography can still look good rests heavily on one film, Nosferatu, which two different sources praise independently, but the broader list of currently good-looking films, Dune, The Substance, Smile, The Brutalist, comes from only one of those two sources.

The argument that financiers and algorithms, not artists, are driving the flat modern look never names an actual financier, studio, or algorithm; it describes an unnamed mechanism rather than a documented one.

The scarcity of Jurassic Park's digital effects is measured in a specific number, about 50 shots, while the modern comparison point is a television show's 2,000 to 3,000 VFX shots; the two numbers come from different kinds of productions made decades apart and are never lined up against a modern feature film's own shot count.

landscape.everyone_does: The same shape shows up across every piece in this material: it opens with a viewer or working cinematographer noticing that modern films look flat or plastic despite bigger budgets, rules out CGI and digital cameras as the simple explanation, then offers a technical or workflow-based reason, dynamic range, lighting choices, lens and camera movement, or fixing things in post, before turning to Jurassic Park as the example of how things used to be done, repeating the roughly 50-digital-shots figure and the practical-effects-first story almost word for word across separate outlets. Business and audience-behavior explanations appear only at the margins, in a comment thread and a single blog post, rather than as a throughline any piece builds around.
landscape.nobody_has: No source in this material includes a current VFX artist or supervisor explaining what a typical shot count or deadline actually looks like on a modern blockbuster, so the claim that artists are spread too thin is asserted from outside rather than confirmed by anyone doing the work. No working director of photography defending a high-dynamic-range or green-screen-heavy approach appears anywhere, so every technical explanation here is critical rather than answered. Nobody with a studio or financing background explains how a modern tentpole's visual style actually gets approved, even though one source blames financiers directly. There is no side-by-side shot count or budget comparison between Jurassic Park and a modern film of similar scale, so the contrast rests on one specific number against a vague one. How audiences now watch films, on phones, laptops, or home HDR televisions, and whether grading for many screen types at once might itself be shaping the flatter look everyone describes, is a question no source raises.

weakest_ground.why: This entire claim about audience tolerance shifting between 1993 and today comes from a single 2013 blog post with no box office data or survey to back up the tolerance claim, so it's the easiest one to push back on.

strongest_ground.why: Four independent sources made for completely different audiences, a VFX breakdown, two historical overviews, and a film blog, all land on the same account: Spielberg planned practical-only, added about 50 digital shots after seeing ILM's tests, and used CGI sparingly.
